§1 — Warm-Up · Quick Fire
Do You Like It? Does She?
Activate food preferences · Introduce Do you like / Does she like · Real context from the office
⏱ 5–8 MIN
Do you like…?
Does she like…?
Do you need…?
What do you want?
☕ Quick hands-up poll: Teacher asks — show of hands. "Do you like coffee?" "Do you like tea?" "Do you like salad for lunch?" Tally on board. Then model: "What does [student] like? She likes coffee — she doesn't like tea." Real students, real answers, instant grammar.
💬 Partner drill (1 min): Ask your partner 3 questions: "Do you like [food]?" Partner: "Yes, I do" or "No, I don't — I prefer [other]." Then report: "My partner likes rice but she doesn't like salad."
🧠 Think first: What's the difference? "I like coffee." vs "Do you like coffee?" vs "Does she like coffee?" — When do you use DO? When DOES? Try to explain before looking at §5.
⚡ Teacher note: S2A introduces question forms for "like." S1 covered statements only. Today's target: Do you like…? / Does he/she like…? + Yes, I do / No, I don't / No, she doesn't. Error to eliminate: "Does she likes?" Write it on the board. Every time a student produces it: tap the board. Students self-correct.
⚡ Quick Win — 20 seconds

Ask the person next to you RIGHT NOW: "Do you like [any food or drink]?" They answer. Swap. Two sentences. You just used today's grammar — before the lesson even started.

Teacher Note — Session Hook

Say: "Last session you told me WHAT you like. Today you ask OTHER PEOPLE — and report what a THIRD person likes. This is the English you need for every team lunch and client dinner."

§2 — Speaking Topic
Team Lunch — What Does Everyone Like?
3 rounds · Do you like / Does he like · Real preferences · 3rd person production
⏱ 8–10 MIN
T-S · Teacher → Student
Teacher interviews each student: "Do you like [food]? Does your manager like [food]?" Student answers with full sentences. Teacher writes one correct sentence per student on the board — builds a class preferences profile.

"Yes, I like salad and chicken. I don't like rice. My manager likes coffee in the morning but she doesn't like tea."
Target: I like + noun · I don't like + noun · She likes + noun · She doesn't like + noun.

S-S · Student — Student
Plan the office team lunch. Ask your partner: "Does your manager like [food]? Do your colleagues like [drink]? What does your team usually eat?" Take notes. Report to class in Round 3.

"My manager likes chicken and rice. She doesn't like salads. My colleagues like coffee — they don't really like tea."
Critical: "She doesn't like" — NOT "She don't like." Board it. Tap it every time.

Class · Report Back
Report what you learned: "[Partner]'s team likes [food]. Her manager likes [food] but doesn't like [food]." Class: raise your hand every time you hear "Does she likes" — that's today's error to eliminate together.

"Ana's team likes chicken and rice. Her manager likes coffee but doesn't like tea. The team doesn't like spicy food."
Pattern to drill: [Name]'s team + likes/doesn't like + noun.

Teacher Note — Error Radar

Two errors to intercept: (1) "Does she likes?" → "Does she like?" — no -s after does in questions. (2) "She don't like" → "She doesn't like." Write both on board. Tap silently when you hear either. Students repeat the corrected version once. Move on.

Teacher Note — "I prefer" as a fixed chunk

"I prefer" is a fixed phrase at A1.1 — not a conjugated verb. Students learn: "I don't like tea. I prefer juice." Don't introduce "She prefers" — that's A1.2. If a student says it, note it as advanced, don't correct harshly.

§4 — Colloquial English
Same 4 Phrases — New Contexts
Review S1 phrases · Apply to new food and office situations · Faster, more natural
⏱ 5 MIN
PHRASE 01 — REVIEW
"Sure, no problem!"
Now use it when a colleague needs an office object. "Can you get me a marker?" "Sure, no problem!" Same phrase, new context — office supplies instead of food.
"Do you need a folder?" "Sure, no problem — here you go!"
PHRASE 02 — REVIEW
"Can I get a…?"
Expand to ALL new drinks and food. "Can I get a juice? A tea? A chicken salad?" Also: "Can I get a folder for these reports?" Natural in any office or cafeteria context.
"Can I get a juice? I'm not really into coffee today."
PHRASE 03 — REVIEW
"Anything else?"
Practice the full mini-dialogue with new food. Worker: "Anything else?" Customer: "Yes, can I also get bread?" or "No, that's all — thanks!" Run it until it's automatic.
"Anything else?" "Yes! Can I get some bread too?" "No, that's all!"
PHRASE 04 — REVIEW
"I'm not really into [rice]."
Use with ALL new food vocabulary today. Works for any noun. Much more natural than "I don't like." At a business lunch — always choose the soft version.
"Do you want rice?" "I'm not really into rice — but I'd like salad!"
Teacher Note — Colloquial Acceleration

Don't re-teach — accelerate. Rapid fire: teacher calls a situation, students say the phrase instantly. "Colleague asks for a stapler." → "Sure, no problem!" "You don't like tea." → "I'm not really into tea." Zero thinking time is the goal.

Teacher Note — GT Original: "beach" and "sheet"

M5 pronunciation alert for Mexican learners. "Beach" = BEE-ch (long EE + CH). "Sheet" = SH + long EE + T. Drill briefly — not as a joke, as professional training. These two words cause real embarrassment at international lunches and meetings. Fixing them now is a professional service.

§5 — Grammar
Like / Need / Want — Questions & Negatives
Do / Does · Don't / Doesn't · Short answers · 3rd person rules · Matching Pairs game
⏱ 12–15 MIN
🚨 Real Situation — Team Lunch Planning

Your US manager emails: "Does everyone like Mexican food? Does Ana like vegetarian options? What does your team usually prefer?"

You know the answers. But how do you write back with the correct grammar forms?

✅ The Grammar Tools

"Do you like Mexican food?" → Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
"Does Ana like vegetarian food?" → Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
"My team likes chicken." → Statement — no do/does.
"She doesn't like salad." → Negative — doesn't + base verb.
"Does he like / Does she like?" → No -s after does in questions!

FormStructureExample
Statement (+)I/you/we/they like · he/she/it likesI like salad. She likes rice.
Negative (−)I don't like · he/she doesn't likeI don't like tea. He doesn't like salad.
Question you/IDo + I/you/we/they + like?Do you like chicken? Do they like juice?
Question he/sheDoes + he/she/it + like?Does she like salad? Does he like coffee?
Short answer (+)Yes, I do. / Yes, she does."Does Ana like tea?" "Yes, she does."
Short answer (−)No, I don't. / No, she doesn't."Does Carlos like salad?" "No, he doesn't."
⚠️ Zero tolerance — correct every single time:
✗ "Does she likes coffee?" → ✅ Does she like coffee? (base verb after does)
✗ "She don't like tea" → ✅ She doesn't like tea (3rd person)
✗ "Do he like salad?" → ✅ Does he like salad? (does with he/she/it)
✗ "Yes, she like it" → ✅ Yes, she does (short answer)
✏️ Activity A — Choose the Correct Form
1. "_____ your manager like salad for lunch?"
2. "My colleague _____ like tea — she prefers juice."
3. "Do you like chicken?" → "_____"
4. "Does Ana like rice?" → "_____"
5. "Do they need folders?" uses "do" — not "does" — because the subject is "they".
✏️ Activity B — True or False: Grammar Rules
"Does she likes coffee?" is correct — you always add -s after does.
"She doesn't like salad" is the correct negative form for he/she/it.
"Does they like rice?" is correct when the subject is "they".
"Yes, she does" is correct as a short answer to "Does she like tea?"
The short answer to "Does Ana want chicken?" is "Yes, she does."

🎴 Matching Pairs — Find the Correct Answer

Teacher Note — Matching Pairs

Tap any card to flip it, then tap another to try to match. Wrong pair = both flash red and flip back. Right pair = both stay green. Find all 6 pairs = badge b2. Run as a race — first to finish wins. Shuffled on every New Game.

🗣️ Micro-Speaking: Write 3 questions about colleagues using "Does [name] like [food]?" Then ask them. Report: "[Name] likes [food] but doesn't like [food]."
§6 — Listening
Ana's Lunch Survey — Celaya Office
Monologue: Ana surveys her team's food preferences · do/does/don't/doesn't throughout
⏱ 8–10 MIN
Lunch Preferences — Vertex Logistics, Celaya
A1.1 · M5 · S2A · Voice: Lauren (ElevenLabs) · Speed: 0.78 · Monologue
0:00 --:--
⚡ First listen: Close notes. What does Ana's team like? What don't they like? What does she need? Answer from memory — then open script.
Hi, my name is Ana García. I'm a project coordinator at Vertex Logistics in Celaya. Today I want to talk about something important for our team: lunch.

I always ask my team: "Do you like the lunch menu today?" It's a simple question, but it's important. My colleague Carlos likes chicken and rice — he always orders the same thing. Does he like salad? No, he doesn't. He doesn't like salad at all. But I like salad! I eat it every day.

Our manager, Daniel, likes tea in the morning. Do I like tea? I'm not really into tea — I prefer coffee. Does Daniel like coffee? Yes, he does, but only in the afternoon.

What does our team need for the office? We need paper every week — we print a lot. We also need markers for the whiteboard. Does everyone need a folder? Yes, they do — we organize all our reports in folders.

This week, I want to organize a team lunch. Do my colleagues like Mexican food? Yes, they do! Does everyone like spicy food? No, not everyone. Carlos doesn't like spicy food. So I need to think about that.

What do I like? I like my team, I like my job, and I really like a good salad with chicken. Perfect lunch!
📎 ElevenLabs: Voice — Lauren (American English) · Speed 0.78 · ~170 words · A1.1 M5 S2A — Ana García, Vertex Logistics, Celaya
Teacher Note — Listening Protocol

Play once without script. Students note: 3 things the TEAM likes, 2 things someone DOESN'T like, 2 things Ana NEEDS. Compare with partner. Second play: open script. Third (optional): read aloud in pairs — one paragraph each. The script uses all forms: do/does/don't/doesn't throughout.

✏️ Comprehension — Multiple Choice
1. What does Carlos like for lunch?
2. What does the team need for the office?
✏️ True or False
Carlos likes salad — he eats it every day.
Ana likes coffee — she's not really into tea.
The whole team likes spicy food.
Ana wants to organize a team lunch this week.
§7 — Production
The Lunch Survey — Real Speaking
Opinion Meter · Survey drill · 60-second report · Timer challenge · Badge b3
⏱ 12–15 MIN
"I regularly talk about food preferences in English at work or with international colleagues."
Disagree50 / 50Agree
50%
Teacher Note — Meter to Production

After voting: "Whoever pressed Agree — name ONE real situation where you talk about food in English." If none: "OK — next week you will. Your US manager visits. You need to coordinate lunch. You need this grammar RIGHT NOW." Creates urgency and real-world relevance for the speaking tasks below.

Question 1 — T-S · Quick Survey
Teacher asks 2 questions per student: "Do you like [food]?" and "Does your manager like [drink]?" Students answer with full short answers + 1 detail. Build the class preference board.
💡 "Do you like salad?" "Yes, I do — I eat it every Tuesday." "Does your manager like tea?" "No, she doesn't — she likes coffee."
Question 2 — S-S · Lunch Planner Roleplay
Student A = company coordinator. Student B = US visitor. A asks what B likes and doesn't like. A recommends a lunch using today's vocabulary. Use: "Do you like…? We have [food]. Does that work?"
💡 A: "Do you like chicken?" B: "Yes, I do." A: "Great — chicken and rice. Do you like salad?" B: "I'm not really into salads. I prefer bread." A: "Sure, no problem!"
Question 3 — Class · Report a Colleague
Each student reports on their partner in 3 sentences: what they like, don't like, and need. Use all 3rd person forms: likes / doesn't like / needs.
💡 "[Name] likes chicken and juice. She doesn't like salad or tea. She needs a marker and folders for her meetings."
Question 4 — 60-second Report ⭐ Challenge
Speak for 60 seconds: describe what YOUR TEAM likes and doesn't like for lunch, and what your office needs this week. Use Do/Does, likes, doesn't like, need, want. No notes. Timer starts now.
💡 "My team likes [food]. Our manager likes [food] but doesn't like [food]. We need [office items]. Does everyone like [item]? Yes, they do!"
Complete 60 seconds → earn badge 📋

🎯 3 Phrases for This Week — Use them starting today
PHRASE 1
"Do you like [food]?"
At the next team lunch, coffee break or client dinner — ask this. 5 words. Opens a real conversation in English. Every international colleague will appreciate it.
PHRASE 2
"She likes [food] but doesn't like [food]."
When coordinating lunch for a visitor, ordering for the team, or writing to a US colleague about food preferences — use this structure. Correct, professional, natural.
PHRASE 3
"I need a [marker/folder/stapler]."
Say this in English every time you need an office object this week. 5 words. It works every time. Stop translating in your head — just say it directly.
